title: Egypt's Mummified Cats Lived Hard Lives, Skulls Show
paragraphs: Cats were sacred in ancient Egypt, and millions were mummified. Researchers in Belgium wanted to know what kind of lives these animals had before they were killed and wrapped.

Wim Van Neer, Bea De Cupere and colleagues studied 131 mummified cat skulls from the burial site of Beni Hassan. They published the work in the Journal of Archaeological Science. Fourteen skulls showed injuries, and nineteen had small holes in the eye sockets, which may point to infection or poor nutrition. About 86 percent of the cats were adults, much more than earlier studies of cat mummies usually found. De Cupere said: "This is not what one would expect for animals destined to become votive mummies."

The team suggests that the cats were kept in crowded conditions, which could have led to stress, fights and disease. However, the researchers only had skulls, not whole skeletons, so the causes of the damage are interpretations and not certain facts.

questions.q: How many skulls did the researchers study?
What might the small holes in the eye sockets show?
Why are the conclusions not certain?
questions.a: The researchers only had skulls, so the causes are interpretations.
